title: The Sky Web: Building a Dome in the Air

chapters.title: Built in the air
narration: Most domes are built from the ground up, a ring at a time, with scaffolding inside. This one is built in the air. A web of cable strung between four trees, and every triangle of the dome hauled up, swung into its place, and left hanging there on three cords, not yet joined to the next. The gasket, the skin and the foundation can wait. Here is how, with every load worked out, and the numbers that argue back.

chapters.title: What is measured, what is assumed
narration: First, what this rests on. The triangles are the solver's own: 40 of them, 869 kilograms of frame, about 1,915 pounds, 21 to 23 kilograms each. Everything else is typed in by a person, with a reason: where the trees stand, how high the ropes are tied, how far they sag, what the rope and the trees will take. 24 figures. Change any of them, and every number after this changes with it.

chapters.title: Four trees, a square
narration: Four trees round the pad, near enough a square, 9 metres a side. The ropes run corner to corner, so each one spans the diagonal: 12.7 metres, about 42 feet. They are tied 8 metres up, 26 feet, on tree-saver straps, never wrapped bare round the bark. Real trees are never a perfect square. The arithmetic only needs the longest diagonal, and the height of the lowest tie.

chapters.title: Two ropes make an X
narration: Two wire ropes, crossing in the middle. Hang the whole frame from the crossing, the worst case, and each rope carries half of 8.5 kilonewtons. A rope that sags 5 percent of its span, 0.64 metres here, pulls on its trees with 21.3 kilonewtons, five times the weight it carries. That flat a rope needs to be half-inch wire rope, worked at a fifth of its strength. Let it sag twice as far and the pull halves, to 10.9: three-eighths rope will do.

chapters.title: What the trees take
narration: And the trees take all of it, eight metres up, as a lever. A 45 centimetre pine, green, bends at about 35 megapascals. Pulled with 21 kilonewtons at the tie, its trunk is worked to a margin of 1.8, and a living tree, which can hide rot, should keep three. So each tree gets a back-guy, to an anchor 8 metres behind it, and that guy pulls 30 kilonewtons: more than the web itself. Or sag the web ten percent, and the margin is 3.7: no guys.

chapters.title: A spiral over the footprint
narration: Then the spiral, woven out from the crossing and seized to the X wherever it crosses. It covers the dome's footprint, a circle 5.9 metres across, but 8 metres above it. The turns are 50 centimetres apart, so a cord thrown up from anywhere under it always lands across a strand. That is 5.9 turns, 55 metres of line, and 24 seizings. The X carries the weight. The spiral only gives the pigtails somewhere to land.

chapters.title: A winch, a block, a hook
narration: A hand winch on the first tree. Its line runs up the trunk to a block at the tie, along under the rope to a pulley at the crossing, and down to a hook. The heaviest triangle is 23 kilograms, a pull of 0.23 kilonewtons, against a winch rated 8.9: 39 times over. One triangle on the hook adds only 0.57 kilonewtons to the X. The weight is the easy part. Getting it where it goes is the work.

chapters.title: A harness that hangs it flat
narration: A triangle comes up in a harness: three legs, one to each corner, meeting in an eye 1 metre above the point the triangle balances on. Hook the eye and it rises flat. The dome has 2 shapes of triangle, so there are 2 harnesses. The one with two short sides needs legs of 1.35 and 1.42 metres; the equal one, three of 1.45. Make them once, label them, and use them forty times.

chapters.title: Up, flat
narration: Up it goes, flat, under the crossing. The hook tops out 6.8 metres up, 22 feet. A hand winch brings in about 3 metres a minute, so a triangle takes 2.3 minutes to raise, and all forty about 1.5 hours of winding. Flat matters: a triangle that tips on the way up catches the line, the X, and anyone underneath.

chapters.title: Swing it out
narration: At the top it hangs from the centre, and its place is somewhere else. A tag line from the ground swings it out from under the crossing, and as it goes it is turned, from flat to the angle it will sit at in the finished dome. The hook stays on. Nothing lets go until the pigtails are on.

chapters.title: Three pigtails over the web
narration: Every triangle carries three pigtails, a cord tied at each corner. Thrown up over the spiral and tied back, they hold it where it is. Then it slips the harness, and the hook goes back for the next. The pigtails are 1.3 to 4.4 metres long, shortest at the crown: 120 of them, 352 metres of cord. Each holds 75 newtons, about 8 kilograms, on a cord that breaks at 9 kilonewtons: 119 times over.

chapters.title: Rim first, crown last
narration: The order matters. The hook comes down at the centre, so the middle has to stay clear until the end: hang the rim first, then the band above it, and the crown last. And the crown is where the hook runs out. With a metre of harness above them, 5 crown triangles would need the hook higher than it can climb. They are hung low, the pigtails go on, and they are hauled the last 44 centimetres by hand, on their own cords.

chapters.title: Forty, floating
narration: And there it is. Forty triangles, each in its place, each on its own three cords, none of them touching. The rim hangs 3.6 metres up, 12 feet, the crown at 6.6. Walk underneath and look up through it. Every seam is still open, every edge is reachable, and nothing is holding anything else up.

chapters.title: Join them later
narration: Joining is later, and it is easy from here. Each triangle swings a little on its cords, so its neighbour can be drawn up to it and the seam closed, a pair at a time, with nothing to lift. When the last seam closes, forty separate triangles are one dome, still hanging where they were.

chapters.title: A taut web is a stiff web
narration: Now the honest part. Trees move in the wind, and they move apart. A rope sagging 5 percent goes straight after its trees lean apart only 8.5 centimetres. After that the rope stretches, and every further centimetre adds about 4 kilonewtons. A storm sways a tree more than that. So the X gets a spring at every end, a heavy tensioner that lets it give, or a slacker sag: at ten percent the trees can spread 34 centimetres before it bites. Hung triangles swing too, once every 2 to 4 seconds.

chapters.title: A second web, higher
narration: Then climb higher, and string a second web over the first, 12 metres up, 39 feet. The same X, the same spiral. But the same pull, half again as high up the trunk, is half again the lever: the trees' margin falls to 1.2, and even a ten percent sag only brings it to 2.4. Up here the guys are not optional.

chapters.title: The first web is in the way
narration: And the first web is in the way. Hung from the second, the crown rises to 10.6 metres, and the first web crosses at 7.4: the dome would have to pass 3.2 metres up through it. So the dome is handed over first. Long cords from the second web, a corner at a time, take the weight. Then the first web comes out: the spiral unwound from its outer end, between the cords, and each rope of the X untied at one tree and pulled through from the other.

chapters.title: A corner at a time
narration: Then up, a corner at a time. The block moves over one corner, the winch raises that side 50 centimetres, its cords are re-tied, and the block moves on to the next. Each step tilts the dome 4.8 degrees and back. 4 metres up is 8 rounds of four: 32 pulls. The heaviest corner is 241 kilograms, 2.4 kilonewtons, still well inside the winch.

chapters.title: Leave it hanging?
narration: And maybe it never comes down. The frame alone, 869 kilograms, is what these ropes were sized for. But a house is not a frame. With its skin, its floor and everything in it, this dome is about 4.6 tonnes, 5.3 times as heavy, and hung from the same X it would pull 113 kilonewtons: more than any rope in the table works to. Living in the trees is a different structure, and it wants an engineer, an arborist, and an inspection every season. This is priced, not rated.

chapters.title: Never under the load
narration: And the rule that matters most. Nobody stands under a triangle on its way up. Dropped from the top of the hoist, 6.8 metres, it lands at 12 metres a second, 41 kilometres an hour, with 1.5 kilojoules. Mark a ring under the hook and keep it empty. Wear a helmet. Climb on a proper climbing system, tied in twice, or hire an arborist for the ties. The web is only as safe as the worst knot in it.

chapters.title: The ground can wait
narration: Two webs, 51 metres of wire rope in the X's, 110 of spiral, 68 of guys, 352 of cord, one winch, two harnesses. Forty triangles hung, joined and raised without a scaffold or a crane, and without ever standing on the thing you are building. The foundation, the gasket and the skin can come later. Or never. Some domes are meant to stay up in the trees.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can
carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from
somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field
with a chainsaw.
